source.method: Each term is a lemma exactly as the hosted morphology tags it; counts are token occurrences in the hosted text, read once at build. Phrases count a head lemma with its partner within two tokens.

groups.title: Messengers and holy ones
groups.note: The words for the beings who stand before the throne and carry its word.

groups.title: The adversary
groups.note: Titles first, names later: the vocabulary of the accuser is mostly common nouns.

groups.title: Demons and unclean spirits
groups.note: What the Gospels cast out, and what the Law says Israel sacrificed to.

groups.title: The deep
groups.note: Where the record puts the end of the story.

terms.note: The ordinary word for a messenger, human or heavenly. The passage, not the word, tells you which is meant.
Greek for messenger, used of heavenly and human messengers alike.
Twice in the New Testament, and never in the plural.
The guardians at Eden's gate, the figures over the ark, and the living beings that carry the throne in Ezekiel.
The Hebrew word carried into Greek letters.
Twice, both in Isaiah's throne vision. The tagged Hebrew keeps it apart from the same letters used for the fiery serpents of the wilderness.
A common noun: an adversary. Used of men, of the angel who blocks Balaam's road, and — with the definite article — of the accuser in Job and Zechariah.
The Hebrew title carried into Greek as a name.
Literally a slanderer. In the letters it also describes people, not only the devil.
The name the Gospels record being thrown at Jesus. Only in Matthew, Mark, and Luke.
Once in the New Testament, in Paul's question to Corinth.
Revelation's word. Its twelfth chapter names the dragon as the old serpent, the devil, and Satan.
The ordinary word for a snake, including the one in Eden.
The ordinary word for a snake. Revelation applies it to the devil as the old serpent.
Twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times of the gods to whom Israel sacrificed.
The New Testament's usual word. Paul uses it of the gods behind pagan sacrifice, as Deuteronomy does.
Once, in Matthew's telling of the swine.
The verb behind “demon-possessed”. Gospels only.
The Gospels' phrase — Mark's especially — for what Jesus casts out.
The spirit that troubled Saul, and the one sent between Abimelech and Shechem.
Mostly Luke's phrase, in his Gospel and in Acts.
The tagged Hebrew separates this sense from the ordinary he-goat. Four times, in the Law, Chronicles, and Isaiah.
Once, in Isaiah's picture of Edom laid waste. The WEB renders “night creature”; the demon Lilith of later Jewish tradition is not in the text.
Only in the Day of Atonement law. Whether it names a place, the sent-away goat, or a desert spirit is disputed; 1 Enoch makes it a fallen angel.
Twice, both in Tobit.
A Roman unit of thousands. Used of the demons at Gerasa and, in Jesus' own mouth, of angels.
In Job, Psalms, and Proverbs a place, set beside Sheol and death. Revelation makes it a name.
Once, as the Hebrew name of the angel of the abyss.
Once, as the Greek of the same name.
In the Greek Old Testament, deep waters. In Revelation, the pit that is opened and shut.
Once, in 2 Peter, of the angels who sinned — the only time the New Testament borrows the Greek name for the underworld.
